title: Exercise: The Whole Body at Work

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Fick principle for whole-body oxygen uptake: VO2 = {{c1::cardiac output x (CaO2 - CvO2)}}.
cards.back: Flow times the oxygen each litre gives up (arterial minus mixed-venous content).
cards.quote: Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction: VO2 = cardiac output x (CaO2 - CvO2)

cards.front: In an incremental exercise test, what is VO2max, and what do laboratories report when there is no clear plateau?
cards.back: VO2max is the ceiling of oxygen uptake: the value that further increases in work rate no longer raise. Without a clear plateau, peak VO2 is reported.
cards.quote: That ceiling is the maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max); without a clear plateau, laboratories report peak VO2.
cards.section: Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction

cards.front: What are the units of absolute VO2 and of mass-specific VO2, and what is the mass-specific form for?
cards.back: Absolute: L per min. Mass-specific: mL per kg of body mass per min, used to compare people of different sizes.
cards.quote: Keep absolute VO2 (L per min) apart from mass-specific VO2 (mL per kg of body mass per min), which compares people of different sizes.
cards.section: Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction

cards.front: In a healthy young adult at rest, give approximate cardiac output, arterial O2 content (CaO2), mixed-venous O2 content (CvO2) and resulting VO2.
cards.back: Cardiac output 5.0 L/min, CaO2 200 mL/L, CvO2 150 mL/L; difference 50 mL/L, so VO2 = 250 mL/min.
cards.why: These are oxygen contents (mL per L of blood), not partial pressures.
cards.quote: At rest: cardiac output 5.0 L/min, CaO2 200 mL/L, CvO2 150 mL/L.
cards.section: Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction

cards.front: Whole-body oxygen extraction fraction is about 25 percent at rest and about {{c1::80}} percent at maximal whole-body exercise.
cards.back: So little room is left on the extraction side at the top.
cards.quote: about 80 percent of each litre's oxygen, against 25 percent at rest

cards.front: Why does the whole-body Fick equation use mixed-venous blood rather than femoral venous blood?
cards.back: Each organ extracts a different share. Femoral venous blood drains one hard-working leg, which extracts more than the body as a whole, so it gives the leg's uptake, not the body's.
cards.quote: femoral venous blood drains one hard-working leg, which extracts more than the body as a whole
cards.section: Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction

cards.front: A healthy 66-kg adult at maximal exercise has heart rate 180 beats/min, stroke volume 110 mL, CaO2 200 mL/L and CvO2 50 mL/L. At rest, cardiac output is 5.0 L/min and the arteriovenous difference is 50 mL/L (VO2 250 mL/min). Find VO2max (absolute and per kg) and split the fold rise into its two factors.
cards.back: Cardiac output 180 x 110 = 19,800 mL/min = 19.8 L/min. Difference 150 mL/L. VO2max = 19.8 x 150 = 2,970 mL/min; 2,970 / 66 = 45.0 mL/kg/min. Fold rise 2,970 / 250 = 11.88 = 3.96 (flow) x 3.0 (extraction).
cards.why: Fold changes multiply; they do not add.
cards.quote: Fold changes multiply; they do not add.
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the rise with Fick

cards.front: Why does splitting a VO2 rise into a cardiac-output factor and an extraction factor not give each factor an independent share?
cards.back: The two factors are linked: more flow through a capillary means less time for each litre to unload, so raising flow tends to lower extraction.
cards.quote: the factors are linked: more flow through a capillary means less time for each litre to unload.
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the rise with Fick

cards.front: At maximal exercise a healthy athlete has cardiac output 22 L/min, CaO2 200 mL/L and an arteriovenous difference of 170 mL/L. If every litre gave up all its oxygen at this cardiac output, how much more VO2 could extraction add?
cards.back: Actual VO2 = 22 x 170 = 3,740 mL/min. Full extraction = 22 x 200 = 4,400 mL/min. 4,400 / 3,740 = 1.18, so at most about 18 percent more; any larger rise must come mostly from delivery.
cards.quote: Even if every litre gave up all 200 mL, uptake at this cardiac output could reach only 19.5 x 200 = 3,900 mL per min, a quarter more.
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the rise with Fick

cards.front: In healthy people at sea level, why does a higher VO2max require more oxygen delivery rather than more extraction?
cards.back: Extraction is already near its limit at maximum (about 80 percent), so it can add little. More uptake needs more flow or more oxygen in each litre.
cards.quote: Extraction can add at most that quarter, so any larger rise has to come mostly from delivery.
cards.section: Worked problem: splitting the rise with Fick

cards.front: During exercise, stroke volume rises with which two factors?
cards.back: Preload (end-diastolic stretch of the ventricle) and contractility (strength of contraction at a given stretch).
cards.quote: Stroke volume rises with preload, the end-diastolic stretch of the ventricle, and contractility
cards.section: Where the extra flow goes

cards.front: In active muscle, contraction can blunt the constricting effect of sympathetic nerves, which is called {{c1::functional sympatholysis}}.
cards.quote: contraction can blunt their constricting effect there, which is called functional sympatholysis.
cards.section: Where the extra flow goes

cards.front: In heavy dynamic exercise, where does most of the extra blood flow to working muscle come from, and what can happen to renal and splanchnic flow?
cards.back: Mostly from the larger cardiac output, not from the gut and kidneys. Sympathetic vasoconstriction can still reduce renal and splanchnic (gut, liver, spleen) flow.
cards.quote: Most of the extra flow to muscle comes from that larger cardiac output, not from the gut and kidneys
cards.section: Where the extra flow goes

cards.front: What is exercise hyperemia, and is a single vasodilator known to explain it?
cards.back: Dilation of active muscle vessels through local signals. No: a 2015 review concluded that no single vasodilator explains it.
cards.quote: Active muscle also dilates through local signals (exercise hyperemia), and a 2015 review concluded that no single vasodilator explains it
cards.section: Where the extra flow goes

cards.front: Healthy subjects did dynamic knee extension with one leg, so the active muscle was essentially one quadriceps, and femoral venous flow was measured by thermodilution. Estimated maximal perfusion was about 2.5 L per kg of active muscle per min. What does this show about the ceiling on whole-body VO2?
cards.back: Estimated maximal perfusion of about 2.5 L per kg of active muscle per min argued against muscle dilator capacity as the ceiling in these subjects; if the heart sets it, small muscle should take far more per kg.
cards.why: It did not test whole-body exercise or the dilator mechanism, and the per-kg figure depends on the estimated quadriceps mass.
cards.quote: the estimated maximal perfusion was about 2.5 L per kg of active muscle per min (per kilogram of quadriceps, not of body mass)
cards.section: How much could muscle take?

cards.front: A small muscle group works maximally while the rest of the body rests, so the heart is not strained. If muscle vessels set the whole-body VO2 ceiling, how should its flow per kg compare with whole-body exercise? What if the heart sets it?
cards.back: Vessels limiting: no more flow per kg than in whole-body exercise, since the vessels are already at their limit. Heart limiting: far more flow per kg, because the muscle no longer shares the cardiac output.
cards.quote: If the heart sets it, the small muscle, freed from sharing the heart, should take far more.
cards.section: How much could muscle take?

cards.front: Assume working muscle can accept 2.5 L per kg per min. A runner uses 15 kg of muscle, maximal cardiac output is 20 L/min, and 85 percent of it reaches the muscle. Compare muscle capacity with delivery.
cards.back: Capacity 2.5 x 15 = 37.5 L/min. Delivery 0.85 x 20 = 17 L/min. Ratio 37.5 / 17 = 2.2: muscle could accept about twice what the heart sends, so the heart, not the vessels, is the main flow limit.
cards.quote: At 2.5 L per kg per min the muscles could accept 2.5 x 20 = 50 L per min.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: the argument in numbers

cards.front: If working muscle could accept several times the blood the heart can send, why are its vessels not fully open at maximal whole-body exercise?
cards.back: Flow equals pressure times conductance. Opening every working muscle fully at maximal cardiac output would collapse arterial pressure, so sympathetic nerves and the baroreflex likely keep muscle partly constricted.
cards.why: This is a leading explanation; how much each contributes is debated.
cards.quote: If every working muscle opened its vessels fully while cardiac output stayed at its maximum, arterial pressure would collapse.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: the argument in numbers

cards.front: Trained men cycled to exhaustion at a constant supramaximal work rate while cardiac output and leg blood flow were measured. What happened to both, and how was it interpreted?
cards.back: Both peaked after about 60 to 90 s and then levelled off while work rate stayed the same. The authors read the plateau as cardiac limits plus muscle vasoconstriction that holds arterial pressure up.
cards.quote: Both peaked after about 60 to 90 seconds and then levelled off, while the work rate stayed the same
cards.section: Why the evidence points to delivery

cards.front: Six weeks of endurance training raised peak VO2 and both blood red-cell volume and muscle mitochondria in untrained men. What manipulation tested which change made the VO2 gain, and what was found?
cards.back: Blood was removed (phlebotomy) until red-cell volume was back at its pretraining value, with muscle adaptations assumed to persist. Peak VO2 fell back to its pretraining level, so in these men the gain rode on delivery.
cards.quote: Yet when red-cell volume was returned to baseline by phlebotomy, the authors report that peak VO2 fell back to its pretraining level.
cards.section: Why the evidence points to delivery

cards.front: Give two cautions that keep the six-week phlebotomy training result from settling whether delivery limits VO2max.
cards.back: Removing blood lowers blood volume (preload, stroke volume) as well as oxygen-carrying capacity, and the experiment cannot say which mattered. A later 10-week study found the gain survived phlebotomy.
cards.quote: Both are delivery, but the experiment cannot say which of the two mattered.
cards.section: Why the evidence points to delivery

cards.front: A healthy person exercises maximally at high altitude, or with anemia. Does delivery still limit VO2max, and through which term of the Fick equation?
cards.back: Yes, delivery still limits, mainly through a lower CaO2 (less oxygen in each litre).
cards.quote: At altitude and in anemia delivery still limits, mainly through a lower CaO2.
cards.section: Why the evidence points to delivery

cards.front: A healthy person at sea level does maximal one-leg knee extension instead of running. Would the rule "delivery, mainly cardiac output, limits peak VO2" apply to the working leg, and why?
cards.back: No. With a small muscle mass the heart has reserve (the one-leg test reached far more flow per kg), so the limit lies elsewhere, not in cardiac output.
cards.why: Rests on the stated scope: the delivery rule does not carry over to small-muscle exercise.
cards.quote: The rule does not carry over to small-muscle exercise, where the heart has reserve and the limit lies elsewhere
cards.section: Why the evidence points to delivery

cards.front: At sea level during low to moderate exercise, about what are arterial PO2 and PCO2?
cards.back: Near their resting values, about 100 and 40 mmHg, because ventilation keeps pace with carbon dioxide output.
cards.quote: arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay near their resting values of about 100 and 40 mmHg at sea level.
cards.section: Breathing protects the oxygen in each litre

cards.front: A healthy adult moves from moderate to heavy exercise, and ventilation now rises faster than carbon dioxide output. Is this hyperventilation, and what happens to arterial PCO2?
cards.back: Yes: hyperventilation means ventilation rising faster than CO2 output. Arterial PCO2 falls. At moderate intensity, by contrast, harder breathing is not hyperventilation.
cards.quote: That can happen in heavy exercise, and then arterial PCO2 falls.
cards.section: Breathing protects the oxygen in each litre

cards.front: In some highly trained runners at sea level, arterial PO2 falls during hard exercise. Predict the effect on VO2max using the Fick equation.
cards.back: Lower PO2 lowers saturation and CaO2, so each litre carries less oxygen; at the same cardiac output and extraction, delivery and VO2max fall. The lung joins the limit through CaO2.
cards.why: In healthy people generally, the lung keeps arterial oxygen up even at maximal work.
cards.quote: There the lung joins the limit through CaO2.
cards.section: Breathing protects the oxygen in each litre

cards.front: A cyclist rides at the same work rate on a hot day as on a cool day and also loses body water as sweat. What happens to stroke volume, what must heart rate do, and what does this mean for muscle?
cards.back: Stroke volume falls, so heart rate must rise to hold cardiac output. In trained cyclists heat plus dehydration still lowered cardiac output by 13 percent; less flow, shared with skin, means less delivery to muscle.
cards.quote: Stroke volume falls, so heart rate would have to rise to hold cardiac output.
cards.section: Heat competes for the flow

cards.front: Why does thermoregulation during exercise compete with working muscle for blood flow?
cards.back: Skin blood flow carries heat from core to skin, where sweat cools only when it evaporates, so skin needs a share of the cardiac output.
cards.quote: Skin blood flow carries heat from the core to the skin, where sweat cools only when it evaporates
cards.section: Heat competes for the flow

cards.front: Name the three factors endurance performance rests on.
cards.back: VO2max, the fraction of it a person can sustain (related to the lactate threshold), and economy, the oxygen cost of moving at a given speed.
cards.quote: Endurance performance rests on three things: VO2max, the fraction of it a person can sustain, and economy
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: Why is lactate described as a fuel rather than waste during exercise?
cards.back: Lactate made from glycolytic pyruvate leaves the fibres that make it and is oxidized by other fibres and the heart, or made into glucose by the liver.
cards.quote: Some glycolytic pyruvate becomes lactate, which leaves the fibres that make it and is oxidized by other fibres and the heart or made into glucose by the liver.
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: The {{c1::lactate threshold}} is the workload above which blood lactate accumulation speeds up as work rises.
cards.back: It has no universal value (not a fixed 4 mmol per L or percentage of VO2max).
cards.quote: The lactate threshold is the workload above which blood lactate accumulation speeds up as work rises.
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: Is the lactate threshold the point where muscle runs out of oxygen? What sets blood lactate concentration?
cards.back: No: muscle keeps consuming oxygen above it. Blood lactate is set by appearance minus clearance; appearance keeps rising with work.
cards.quote: It is not where oxygen runs out; muscle keeps consuming oxygen above it.
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: Suppose training raises a person's lactate clearance capacity while lactate appearance at each work rate is unchanged. Predict the effect on the lactate threshold and on the fraction of VO2max that can be sustained.
cards.back: The threshold should shift to a higher work rate, since blood lactate climbs only when appearance outpaces clearance; the sustainable fraction is related to the threshold, so would probably rise.
cards.why: Rests on blood lactate = appearance minus clearance, and on the sustainable fraction being related to the threshold. Trained men did show higher clearance at their threshold, but as an association.
cards.quote: Blood lactate is set by appearance minus clearance.
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: In trained subjects, how does fuel use change as exercise intensity rises?
cards.back: Plasma glucose uptake and muscle glycogen oxidation rise with intensity; total fat oxidation is highest at a middle intensity.
cards.quote: plasma glucose uptake and muscle glycogen oxidation rose with intensity, and total fat oxidation was highest at a middle intensity
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: During prolonged exercise, how do plasma insulin and glucagon change, and how does contracting muscle still take up more glucose?
cards.back: Insulin falls and glucagon rises, favouring glucose release from the liver. Contracting muscle takes up more glucose by a route that does not require insulin.
cards.quote: During prolonged exercise plasma insulin falls and glucagon rises, favouring glucose release from the liver
cards.section: What the ceiling is for: fuel, lactate and the fraction you can hold

cards.front: Young men trained leg extension for six weeks with heavy or light loads. Muscle thickness rose similarly in both, but strength and voluntary activation rose more with the heavy load. What does this suggest?
cards.back: A neural contribution to strength gains: the heavy load improved how fully the nervous system drives the muscle, beyond any change in muscle size.
cards.quote: heavy and light loads raised muscle thickness similarly, but strength and voluntary activation
cards.section: What training changes

cards.front: Why is peak cardiac output low in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
cards.back: Peak stroke volume is low and rises little (weak contractility), and peak heart rate is often lower than in a healthy person of the same age.
cards.quote: peak stroke volume is low and rises little (weak contractility) and peak heart rate is often lower
cards.section: Heart failure: the Fick split as a diagnostic

cards.front: At the same submaximal work rate, a patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and a healthy control both take up 0.9 L O2/min with CaO2 200 mL/L. Cardiac output is 6 L/min in the patient and 9 L/min in the control. Find each one's arteriovenous difference and mixed-venous content, and say whose lactate is higher.
cards.back: Difference = VO2 / flow: 900 / 6 = 150 mL/L (patient) vs 900 / 9 = 100 mL/L (control). CvO2 = 200 - 150 = 50 vs 100 mL/L. Lactate is higher in the patient: underperfused muscle accumulates lactate at a lower absolute work rate.
cards.quote: Each litre of the patient's smaller flow must give up more oxygen.
cards.section: Heart failure: the Fick split as a diagnostic

cards.front: Besides low peak cardiac output, what limits exercise in chronic heart failure?
cards.back: Reduced oxygen transport from blood into muscle (partly from more sympathetic constriction) and muscle changes: lower mitochondrial volume and enzymes, in some studies fewer capillaries per fibre, and a fibre-type shift.
cards.why: Ventilation per litre of CO2 output is also higher. Flow is the first problem, but the muscle adds a limit of its own.
cards.quote: Here the guiding rule bends: flow is the first problem, but the muscle adds a limit of its own.
cards.section: Heart failure: the Fick split as a diagnostic

cards.front: Exercise at a fixed pace on a hot day instead of a cool one: skin takes a share of cardiac output. If cardiac output does not rise to compensate, what happens to muscle delivery?
cards.back: Muscle gets less flow, because skin shares the same cardiac output; less delivery to muscle follows. The lesson does not state a heart failure result.
cards.why: Heat competing with muscle for a shared cardiac output; conditional on output not rising to compensate.
cards.quote: Less flow, shared with the skin, means less delivery to muscle.
cards.section: Heat competes for the flow

cards.front: Design an experiment in trained cyclists to test whether the work of the breathing muscles at maximal cycling takes blood flow from the legs. Give the manipulation, key measurements and how to read the result.
cards.back: Hold power near maximum; on separate randomized visits unload inspiration with a ventilator, add inspiratory resistance, or use sham. Measure leg flow, arterial pressure, cardiac output, blood gases. Competition: unloading raises leg flow, loading lowers it.
cards.why: Cardiac output must be measured, because if it rose to supply both, leg flow would not change.
cards.quote: If breathing competes for flow, unloading should raise leg flow and conductance and loading should lower them.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Unloading inspiratory work during maximal cycling in trained men raised leg blood flow, yet a follow-up found cardiac output about 9 percent lower with unloading. What does the combination show?
cards.back: Unloading did not simply move a fixed cardiac output to the legs: cardiac output was about 9 percent lower with unloading, and the authors estimated up to 14 to 16 percent of output goes to the breathing muscles. Leg resistance tracked noradrenaline spillover, fitting a proposed respiratory-muscle reflex.
cards.why: Seven trained men at maximal exercise say nothing about moderate exercise or women.
cards.quote: so unloading did not simply move a fixed cardiac output to the legs
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An anemic person has hemoglobin 120 g/L, 97 percent saturated, at arterial PO2 100 mmHg. Using 1.34 mL O2 per g Hb and 0.03 mL per L per mmHg dissolved, calculate CaO2.
cards.back: Bound: 1.34 x 120 x 0.97 = 156 mL/L. Dissolved: 0.03 x 100 = 3 mL/L. CaO2 = about 159 mL/L, against about 198 with 150 g/L hemoglobin.
cards.quote: Dissolved oxygen at a PO2 of 100 mmHg adds 0.03 mL per L per mmHg x 100 = 3 mL per L.
cards.section: Checking CaO2

cards.front: In a simple model of capillary oxygen unloading, how does the leverage of delivery versus the muscle side change with the extraction fraction, and why does this matter for heart failure and small-muscle exercise?
cards.back: Once extraction is high, delivery has more leverage than the muscle side, though extra delivery buys less than its full share. At lower extraction the muscle side gains weight, the better picture for heart failure and small-muscle exercise.
cards.why: These are model outputs, not measurements.
cards.quote: at lower extraction the muscle side gains weight, the better picture for heart failure and small-muscle exercise.
cards.section: How much does more flow buy?
